_comment: ZeroBreach detection signatures, externalized from ZeroBreach-V23.ps1 so the engine's script body contains no malware-signature literals (avoids AMSI/Defender false positives). Loaded at runtime via Get-Content|ConvertFrom-Json — data files are not AMSI-scanned. Edit signatures here without touching the engine.
_comment_email_content_rules: Content-based signatures for HTML/JS phishing trojans (HTML smuggling, JS redirectors, obfuscated droppers). Applied to the CONTENT of small html/htm/js/hta/vbs/svg/log files found in email-attachment caches (Phase 74.5) and user paths (Phase 90). These match real malicious constructs, NOT antivirus signature NAMES, so they survive renaming and have low false-positive rates.
_comment_email_scan: Paths and extensions for Phase 74.5 (email-attachment malware scan). Paths use env-var tokens expanded at runtime. Deliberately EXCLUDES the bulk Outlook OST/PST data store (multi-GB, scanned separately) and targets only attachment-extraction / diagnostic caches where extracted trojans land.
_comment_proactive_hardening: Adversary-informed PROACTIVE safeguards. Each entry is a foothold a real attacker plants/abuses for execution, persistence or privilege escalation. Phase 74.7 audits these even when no active infection is found, so a freshly-cleaned box is hardened against re-infection rather than only scanned reactively.

proactive_persistence_regs.Why: Run-once autorun, often used by droppers
Load/Run values execute at logon (legacy but abused)

proactive_office_keys.Name: Level
proactive_office_keys.Why: Outlook attachment security level — lower = unsafe attachments openable

proactive_office_keys.Name: VBAWarnings
proactive_office_keys.Why: Word macro security — 2 = block macros from internet/email-sourced docs, prompt for local trusted ones (does NOT break legit internal macros)

proactive_office_keys.Name: VBAWarnings
proactive_office_keys.Why: Excel macro security — 2 = block internet/email-sourced macros, prompt for local trusted ones

_comment_fp_allowlists: False-positive allowlists (NOT malware signatures). Used to suppress/downgrade benign-but-noisy matches. Regex fragments are matched case-insensitively against file paths/names or cert subjects. Tune here without touching the engine.
_comment_runkey_benign_values: Phase 20: matched against 'name = value' of Run/RunOnce entries. OneDrive writes its own cleanup RunOnce values (cmd.exe+del of its cached updater) — benign, downgraded to POSSIBLE/Info (never auto-DeleteReg). Patterns MUST pin the ENTIRE value to the exact benign command shape ($-anchored, no room for chained commands) or malware can name its value to self-allowlist. Covers both the machine-wide (\Microsoft OneDrive\) and per-user (\Microsoft\OneDrive\) install paths.
_comment_miner_config_benign_paths: Phase 63: config.json content heuristics (pools/stratum/mining words) hit legitimate app configs — LGHUB game-integration applets et al. Allowlisted parent paths downgrade to POSSIBLE/Info.
_comment_spooler_benign_dlls: Phase 96: Microsoft printer RESOURCE DLLs in spool\drivers are catalog-signed (invisible to Get-AuthSig, which only sees embedded Authenticode) and grade as UNSIGNED on every box with a PCL/PS driver. Known resource-DLL names downgrade to POSSIBLE/Info.
_comment_keylogger_benign_paths: Phase 48: keystroke-log *name* heuristics (*typed*, *capture*log*, …) inside package-manager trees are library files (e.g. py.typed markers), not keylogger output. Downgraded to POSSIBLE/Info.
_comment_yara_benign_paths: Phase 90: JIT/renderer runtime DLLs legitimately contain VirtualAllocEx/WriteProcessMemory-class API strings (SwiftShader et al. compile shaders at runtime); package-manager trees ship API-name-bearing sources. Rule hits here downgrade to POSSIBLE/Info instead of HIGH/DeleteFile.
_comment_sct_benign_paths: Phase 94: .sct/.wsc scriptlets inside package-manager trees are library test fixtures (e.g. pywin32's Testpys.sct), not Squiblydoo staging. Downgraded to POSSIBLE/Info.
_comment_c2_named_pipe_regex: Named-pipe backdoor patterns (Phase 62). Specific C2/RAT framework pipe names + known-malware terms ONLY. Must NOT include a broad hex/GUID match — most legit Windows RPC/COM/Ep-mapper pipes are GUID- or hex-named, so a catch-all floods CRITICAL false positives.
_comment_hidden_task_benign_paths: Scheduled-task FullNames (Phase 104) that legitimately ship <Hidden>true</Hidden> maintenance tasks. Matched case-insensitively against the task XML's full path. Known = INFO; unrecognized hidden tasks are NOT suppressed — they downgrade to POSSIBLE (surfaced for review, never auto-deleted). A hidden task is weak signal on its own.
_comment_bits_suspicious_remote: BITS job (Phase 31) escalation indicators. A BITS job is corroborating evidence, not a standalone HIGH (every Windows/app updater uses BITS). Default POSSIBLE; escalate to HIGH only when the job's remote URL is a raw IP, or it stages an executable/script into a user-writable path. NOT malware signatures — generic heuristics.
_comment_ws1_externalized: WS1 (2026-06-30): inline name-lists that read like AV signatures, moved out of engine/*.ps1 so the script body carries no signature literals (AMSI/portability hardening). Each key maps 1:1 to one phase. Content is the exact pre-externalization list — refreshing/expanding these families is WS2.
_comment_ws2_expansion: WS2 (2026-06-30): detection-coverage expansion researched from public sources (MITRE, abuse.ch, CISA #StopRansomware, LOLDrivers, LOLBAS, SigmaHQ, vendor reports). All DATA / AMSI-safe. Point-in-time C2 domains/hashes are confirmation IOCs (many sinkholed) — the durable signals are the behavior rules, drop-path rules, ransom-note filenames, BYOVD driver names, and anchored C2 pipe regexes. Severities deliberately conservative.

byovd_cert_tbs_hashes.Note: Cert TBS hash — durable across the ~2500 polymorphic 8-byte-modified variants where SHA256 is useless

_comment_browser_policy_keys: Phase 116. Enterprise browser policy keys that adware/stealers abuse. A force-installed extension survives a user uninstall, which is exactly why hijackers use it — but MSP-managed fleets set these legitimately, so the finding is Info/POSSIBLE and never auto-acted-on.
_comment_browser_policy_disable_values: Phase 116. Browser safety controls turned OFF by policy — a hallmark of adware installers and of an operator being set up for a drive-by.

browser_policy_disable_values.name: SafeBrowsingEnabled
browser_policy_disable_values.desc: Chrome Safe Browsing disabled by policy

browser_policy_disable_values.name: SmartScreenPuaEnabled
browser_policy_disable_values.desc: Edge PUA blocking disabled by policy

browser_policy_disable_values.name: DownloadRestrictions
browser_policy_disable_values.desc: Chrome dangerous-download blocking relaxed by policy

_comment_browser_pref_rules: Phase 116. Content rules for Chromium 'Preferences' / 'Secure Preferences'. Off-store update_url is how sideloaded adware extensions self-update.
_comment_firefox_policy_rules: Phase 116. Firefox policies.json / user.js tamper. Deliberately POSSIBLE — managed fleets ship policies.json on purpose.
_comment_browser_arg_abuse_rules: Phase 116/117. Chromium command-line switches abused for session theft. Matched against RUNNING browser command lines and against .lnk shortcut arguments.

browser_arg_abuse_rules.Name: Browser-RemoteDebuggingPort
browser_arg_abuse_rules.Why: CDP cookie/session theft — an attacker attaches to the live browser and reads decrypted cookies without touching the DPAPI store

browser_arg_abuse_rules.Name: Browser-LoadUnpackedExtension
browser_arg_abuse_rules.Why: loads an unpacked extension straight off disk, bypassing the web store

browser_arg_abuse_rules.Name: Browser-HeadlessDumpDom
browser_arg_abuse_rules.Why: scripted headless scrape of an authenticated session

browser_arg_abuse_rules.Name: Browser-ProxyServerOverride
browser_arg_abuse_rules.Why: routes all browsing through an attacker proxy

browser_arg_abuse_rules.Name: Browser-AltUserDataDir
browser_arg_abuse_rules.Why: throwaway profile in Temp — typical of automated credential harvesting

_comment_native_messaging_keys: Phase 117. A native-messaging host lets a browser extension execute a local binary. Malicious extensions register one to get code execution outside the sandbox.
_comment_native_messaging_benign_hosts: FP allowlist (Phase 117) — password managers, PDF/meeting/AV vendors and browser vendors all legitimately register native-messaging hosts.
_comment_lnk_hijack_rules: Phase 118. Malicious .lnk payloads. LNK is the #1 phishing container since Office macros were blocked by default (2022) — the icon says 'document', the target says 'powershell'.
_comment_sideload_dll_names: Phase 119. Known DLL-sideloading targets: a signed application resolves these by name, so dropping an unsigned copy next to the EXE gets attacker code running under the app's identity and reputation. The phase only flags an UNSIGNED copy of one of these sitting beside a SIGNED executable.
_comment_sideload_scan_roots_raw: Phase 119. User-writable roots only. Program Files needs admin to write, so a sideload there is already covered by the System32/binary-integrity phases.
_comment_sideload_benign_paths: FP allowlist (Phase 119). Per-user app installers legitimately ship private copies of these runtime DLLs; several are catalog-signed only, which Get-AuthSig reports as unsigned.
_comment_electron_app_paths_raw: Phase 120. Electron apps keep their program code in USER-WRITABLE AppData, so malware can patch the app itself with no admin rights and no new autostart entry. Token/seed stealers do exactly this to Discord and to desktop crypto wallets.
_comment_electron_tamper_rules: Phase 120. Content rules for injected Electron loaders (index.js / preload / *.asar sidecars). BetterDiscord-class client mods are POSSIBLE only — many users install them deliberately.
_comment_office_addin_keys: Phase 121. COM/VSTO add-ins load into Office at every start. LoadBehavior 3 = load-at-startup.
_comment_office_perf_keys: Phase 121. The 'Office test' key is a pure-backdoor persistence primitive — no product ever creates it.

office_perf_keys.desc: Office 'test\Special\Perf' key — loads an arbitrary DLL into EVERY Office application at launch. It has no legitimate use outside Microsoft debugging.
Office 'test\Special\Perf' key (machine-wide) — loads an arbitrary DLL into EVERY Office application at launch.
Office 'test\Special\Perf' key (WOW64) — loads an arbitrary DLL into EVERY Office application at launch.

_comment_office_template_paths_raw: Phase 121. Global template / startup folders: anything dropped here runs on every document open. Normal.dotm carrying macros is the classic Office persistence.
_comment_office_addin_extensions: Phase 121. XLL/WLL are native DLLs Excel/Word load by extension — they bypass the macro trust prompt entirely and became the dominant Office malware format after macro blocking.
_comment_office_addin_benign_paths: FP allowlist (Phase 121). Finance/compliance/e-signature suites all ship real Office add-ins; so does the RMM tooling this product treats as partner software.
_comment_monitored_app_roots_raw: Phase 122. Per-user application installs live in writable directories, so 'the app itself was swapped' is a real and quiet persistence route. Flags an executable whose Authenticode signature is invalid/HashMismatch, i.e. patched after signing.
_comment_exec_evidence_suspect_path_rege: Phase 123. BAM/DAM and UserAssist record what actually EXECUTED, with timestamps — the single best 'did something run?' artifact on Windows, and it survives the payload deleting itself. This pattern is the user-writable-path shape that legitimate installed software does not have.
_comment_exec_evidence_benign_paths: FP allowlist (Phase 123). Installers, updaters, packaged Python/Electron apps and the RMM agents all legitimately execute out of these paths.
_comment_clickfix_runmru_rules: Phase 124. 'ClickFix' / fake-CAPTCHA / fake-update social engineering: the page tells the victim to press Win+R and paste a command, so the payload is typed by the USER and lands in HKCU RunMRU. That key is often the only surviving evidence of initial access. The paste is padded with a fake 'verification' comment so the real command scrolls out of the Run box — hence the marker rule.
_comment_clipper_wallet_rules: Phase 125. A clipboard clipper carries a TABLE of attacker wallet addresses and swaps whatever the victim copies. One address in a file is noise; several distinct chains inside one small user-path binary/script is the clipper shape — the phase requires that multi-chain/multi-address density before reporting.
_comment_clipper_api_rules: Phase 125. Clipboard API usage alone is benign (every password manager does it) — only reported when it co-occurs with a wallet-address table in the same user-path file.
_comment_extended_autostart_points: Phase 126. The autostart locations beyond Run/Services/Tasks. Each entry carries the STOCK Windows value where one exists, so the phase reports a delta rather than the presence of a normal OS feature.

extended_autostart_points.desc: AppCertDlls — every DLL listed here is loaded into EVERY process that calls CreateProcess. Windows ships this key EMPTY.

extended_autostart_points.name: BootExecute
extended_autostart_points.desc: BootExecute runs native images before Win32 starts. Stock value is exactly 'autocheck autochk *'.

extended_autostart_points.name: Authentication Packages
extended_autostart_points.desc: LSA authentication packages load into lsass.exe with SYSTEM rights — a classic credential-theft persistence.

extended_autostart_points.name: Notification Packages
extended_autostart_points.desc: Password-filter DLLs see every password change in CLEARTEXT.

extended_autostart_points.name: Security Packages
extended_autostart_points.desc: SSP DLLs load into lsass.exe (mimikatz 'memssp' abuses exactly this).
Netsh helper DLLs load whenever netsh.exe runs — including from scripts and RMM tooling.
Print-monitor DLLs load into spoolsv.exe as SYSTEM at boot.
extended_autostart_points.default: Local Port|Standard TCP/IP Port|USB Monitor|WSD Port|BJ Language Monitor|PJL Language Monitor|Microsoft Shared Fax Monitor|AppMon|LPR Port

extended_autostart_points.desc: Time-provider DLLs load into the SYSTEM w32time service.
Active Setup StubPath runs once per user at first logon — a quiet way to seed every profile on a shared box.

extended_autostart_points.name: SCRNSAVE.EXE
extended_autostart_points.desc: Screensaver hijack — any .scr here runs after the idle timeout.

extended_autostart_points.name: AppInit_DLLs
extended_autostart_points.desc: AppInit_DLLs loads into every user-mode process linking user32.dll.

extended_autostart_points.name: Taskman
extended_autostart_points.desc: Winlogon Taskman replaces the shell task manager launched at logon.

extended_autostart_points.name: GinaDLL
extended_autostart_points.desc: GinaDLL is a legacy credential-interception hook; modern Windows never sets it.

extended_autostart_points.name: StartupPrograms
extended_autostart_points.desc: Terminal Services StartupPrograms runs on every RDP logon.

extended_autostart_points.name: Debugger
extended_autostart_points.desc: A Debugger value on explorer.exe hijacks the shell itself.

extended_autostart_points.name: ReflectDebugger
extended_autostart_points.desc: WER ReflectDebugger is executed by the error-reporting service; used as a stealth launcher.

extended_autostart_points.name: UserInitMprLogonScript
extended_autostart_points.desc: UserInitMprLogonScript runs a script at every logon and is set per-user with no admin rights.

extended_autostart_points.name: AutoRun
extended_autostart_points.desc: Command Processor AutoRun executes on EVERY cmd.exe launch.

extended_autostart_points.name: AutoRun
extended_autostart_points.desc: Command Processor AutoRun (per-user) executes on EVERY cmd.exe launch.

_comment_winsock_lsp_benign: FP allowlist (Phase 126) — the Winsock catalog entries Windows ships. A third-party LSP is legacy AV/VPN behaviour, so it is reported POSSIBLE, not removed.
_comment_shell_extension_keys: Phase 127. A shell extension is a DLL Explorer loads into ITSELF. Malware registers one for persistence that survives every autorun cleanup, because nobody looks here.

shell_extension_keys.desc: per-user context-menu handlers for ALL file types
shell service objects loaded by explorer at logon

_comment_shell_extension_benign_dlls: FP allowlist (Phase 127). Cloud-sync clients (OneDrive/Dropbox/Box), archivers and version-control shells all legitimately install overlay/context-menu handlers.
_comment_remote_access_products: Phase 128. Attackers install legitimate remote-access software rather than a RAT because it is signed, allowlisted and looks like IT. NetSupport Manager in particular is redistributed as 'NetSupport RAT'. This phase INVENTORIES what is installed and reports it for operator judgement — it never auto-acts, because on an MSP fleet several of these ARE the management tooling.
_comment_remote_access_partner_vendors: Rule #2 (CLAUDE.md): Datto / CentraStage / Kaseya and peer RMM platforms are legitimate partner tooling. A product on this list is reported as INVENTORY (INFO), not as a threat, unless an independent malicious signal is present.
_comment_remote_access_suspicious_contex: Phase 128. A remote-access tool running out of Temp/Public/Recycle-Bin, or under a one-to-three-character name, is not an IT deployment.
_comment_exfil_staging_tools: Phase 129. rclone is the single most common ransomware exfiltration tool — double-extortion crews copy the file shares to cloud storage before encrypting. All of these are legitimate admin utilities, so presence alone is POSSIBLE/Info; the signal is a config pointing at an unknown remote plus staged archives.
_comment_exfil_config_rules: Phase 129. An rclone.conf with a configured cloud remote on an endpoint that is not a backup server is the exfil-staging tell.
_comment_exfil_archive_rules: Phase 129. Split multi-volume archives in a user-writable path are how a large data set is moved through a size-limited channel.
_comment_webhook_c2_rules: Phase 130. Living-off-trusted-sites C2. A stealer does not need infrastructure: it POSTs the loot to a Discord webhook or a Telegram bot, both of which are TLS to a domain no proxy blocks. A hard-coded webhook URL inside a user-path script or binary is close to a zero-FP signal.
_comment_webhook_c2_benign_paths: FP allowlist (Phase 130). API tooling and package trees legitimately carry webhook URL patterns in samples and tests. The chat clients themselves are deliberately NOT listed: allowlisting AppData\\Roaming\\discord\\ suppressed the one case the phase's client-core Quarantine branch exists for (a token stealer patched into the client), and no legitimate client build embeds a concrete webhook URL with a 50+ char token.
_comment_packed_script_indicators: Phase 131. Compiled-script droppers. The interpreter is signed and clean; the malice is in the script blob beside it, so AV verdicts on the EXE are useless. Everything here is POSSIBLE/Info unless it is co-located with a matching script blob in a user-writable path.

packed_script_indicators.Name: AutoIt-CompiledScript
packed_script_indicators.Why: compiled AutoIt script — DarkGate and a long tail of loaders ship as AutoIt3.exe + .a3x

packed_script_indicators.Name: AutoIt-Interpreter
packed_script_indicators.Why: the AutoIt interpreter itself dropped into a user path

packed_script_indicators.Name: AutoHotkey-Interpreter
packed_script_indicators.Why: AutoHotkey interpreter in a user path — used the same way as AutoIt

packed_script_indicators.Name: AutoHotkey-Script
packed_script_indicators.Why: AutoHotkey script alongside a dropped interpreter

packed_script_indicators.Name: Nim-Nuitka-PyInstaller-Marker
packed_script_indicators.Why: script packed into an EXE — legitimate for tooling, but the standard way to ship a Python/Nim stealer

_comment_packed_script_benign_paths: FP allowlist (Phase 131). Real AutoIt/AutoHotkey/Python installs and packaged-app extraction dirs.
_comment_webshell_roots_raw: Phase 132. Web-root and Exchange auth directories. ProxyShell/ProxyLogon dropped .aspx shells into owa\auth, and that shape has been copied by everything since. Skipped silently on a box with no web server.
_comment_webshell_extensions: Phase 132. Server-side script extensions worth content-scanning inside a web root.
_comment_webshell_content_rules: Phase 132. Web-shell constructs, not AV signature names: every one of these is 'take a value straight from the HTTP request and execute it', which no legitimate page does.
_comment_wiper_procs: Phase 133. Wipers masquerade as ransomware but have no recovery path, so telling them apart changes the entire incident response. sdelete64 is Sysinternals — legitimate, but its presence during an active incident is worth stating.
_comment_destructive_behavior_rules: Phase 133. Destructive-intent command shapes. Reported against process command lines and dropped scripts.

destructive_behavior_rules.Name: Destructive-BootRecordRewrite
destructive_behavior_rules.Why: boot record manipulation (also a legitimate repair step)

_comment_lateral_movement_artifacts: Phase 133. Lateral-movement residue. On a single endpoint this is the evidence that the box was reached FROM somewhere else — which changes the scope of the incident from one machine to the network.

lateral_movement_artifacts.Name: PsExec service binary
lateral_movement_artifacts.Why: a PsExec-class service binary in System32 means someone executed code on this box remotely

lateral_movement_artifacts.Name: Impacket random service
lateral_movement_artifacts.Why: impacket's smbexec/atexec create an 8-random-character service binary

lateral_movement_artifacts.Name: Admin share write
lateral_movement_artifacts.Why: administrative-share access, the transport under PsExec/impacket

_comment_hunt_task_benign_paths: Phase 134 allowlist. Task tree paths Windows itself churns or ships without a readable SD. Anchored with ^\\ to a full task path, never a bare name.
_comment_hunt_service_benign_names: Phase 135 allowlist. Per-user service TEMPLATE instances carry a transient _<luid> suffix and never appear in Win32_Service under the template name.
_comment_hunt_ppid_benign_paths: Phase 136 allowlist. Session and job managers whose children are legitimately re-parented, which makes creation-order comparison meaningless for them.
_comment_hunt_driver_benign_names: Phase 138 allowlist. Boot-start storage and filter drivers that legitimately unload once the boot phase completes, so registered-but-not-loaded is their normal steady state.
_comment_hunt_timestomp_benign_paths: Phase 139 allowlist. Package extraction and build trees copy second-resolution timestamps wholesale, which is the same artifact a timestomping tool leaves.
_comment_hunt_filename_benign_paths: Phase 140 allowlist. Localization resource trees legitimately carry non-ASCII filenames; nothing here allows a bidi override, which is checked on the leaf name and has no benign use in an executable.
_comment_hunt_memory_benign_paths: Phases 141/143 allowlist. An EDR is, by every signal these phases look for, a legitimate rootkit: it injects unbacked code into everything it protects. Flagging the customer's own security product as an implant is the fastest way to teach an operator to ignore this band. Datto/CentraStage/Kaseya are partner RMM tooling per CLAUDE.md rule #2.
_comment_system_image_names: Phase 144. Core Windows binary filenames (WITH extension, lowercase). A process carrying one of these names from outside \\Windows\\System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS\\ is masquerading (T1036.005). Anchored whole-name at load, never substring.
_comment_killchain_stages: Phase 160. Maps a finding's ThreatType/Group/Phase text to a kill-chain stage. A correlated chain spanning several DISTINCT stages is an intrusion; several findings in one stage are usually one artifact described several ways. Patterns are matched case-insensitively against the concatenation of ThreatType, Group and Phase.
